Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 – Oncological strategy  
- Perform curative‑intent resection of the symptomatic left‑sided colon primary (standard oncologic left hemicolectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
- Because the liver metastases are limited (two lesions ≤3 cm, located in segments II and V) and the patient has no extra‑hepatic disease, plan a curative liver resection. Options:  
   • Simultaneous colon and liver resection in a single operative session, provided the surgical team has experience with combined procedures and the patient’s physiologic reserve is adequate.  
   • Staged approach: colon resection first, allow 4–6 weeks recovery, then perform parenchymal‑sparing liver surgery (segment II wedge resection or left lateral sectionectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy) to achieve negative margins while preserving future liver remnant.  
- Post‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) should be administered after recovery from surgery, given the high CEA and tumor size, to address micrometastatic disease.  
- If recurrence occurs, consider repeat hepatic resection or ablative therapies; the RAS‑wild‑type status allows future anti‑EGFR‑containing regimens if needed.  

Step 2 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  

Step 3 – Missing data  
No essential data are missing; the provided information (primary tumor size and location, number and size of hepatic lesions, absence of extra‑hepatic disease, RAS wild‑type status, performance status not limited) is sufficient to make a definitive recommendation.

Step 1 – Oncological strategy  
- Urgent surgical control of the symptomatic left‑sided colon cancer: standard oncologic left hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis (or diverting stoma if intra‑operative concern for anastomotic safety).  
- Post‑operative recovery (≈7‑10 days) followed by peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy. Because the tumour is RAS‑wild type, a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody is appropriate; 3–6 cycles are commonly given before liver surgery (conversion/downsizing is not required but provides early systemic control and a test of tumour biology).  
- Restaging contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) after chemotherapy to confirm that the two hepatic lesions remain resectable and that no new extra‑hepatic disease has appeared.  
- Curative‑intent hepatic resection: segment II (or left lateral sectionectomy) and segment V wedge/segmentectomy, aiming for R0 margins ≥1 mm, preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and an FLR > 30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver.  
- Optional: If intra‑operative assessment after colon resection shows excellent physiologic reserve, adequate FLR and no technical concerns, a simultaneous colon‑first/ liver‑second approach could be performed; otherwise a staged approach as outlined above is preferred.  

Step 2 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  

The two liver metastases (2.2 cm in segment II, 3 cm in segment V) can be removed with a limited hepatectomy while preserving sufficient functional liver remnant; there is no extra‑hepatic disease and the primary tumour is amenable to curative resection.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and calculation of future liver remnant volume (CT volumetry or MRI).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and cardiopulmonary assessment (e.g., ECG, spirometry) to confirm fitness for major abdominal surgery.  
- Detailed operative risk assessment (ASA grade, nutritional status).  

If these data are within acceptable limits, the above plan can be implemented safely.

- After postoperative recovery (typically 2–3 weeks), obtain a dedicated liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define lesion anatomy, vascular relationships and future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
- If MRI confirms that both metastases can be removed with ≤2 segmental resections and an adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver), proceed to liver surgery. Options:  
   • Simultaneous colon and liver resection in the same operative session (feasible because the colon operation is limited and the hepatic resections are minor).  
   • Staged approach (colon first, then liver resection within 4–6 weeks) if intra‑operative assessment suggests increased risk (e.g., borderline FLR, complex vascular anatomy).  
- Because the disease is synchronous but limited and RAS‑wild‑type, give peri‑operative systemic therapy:  
   • Consider 3 months of neoadjuvant FOLFOX (± bevacizumab) before liver resection if FLR is borderline or if there is concern about occult micrometastatic disease.  
   • If liver resection is performed promptly after colon surgery, give adjuvant FOLFOX for 6 months after both resections.  
- Continue postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 2 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – definitive surgical planning requires a liver MRI to assess vascular involvement and an FLR volume calculation; these data are currently missing and are decisive for confirming safe resection.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary colon tumor.  
- Detailed hepatic vascular anatomy and any tumor‑vessel contact (portal/hepatic artery).  
- Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI findings (lesion morphology, relationship to vessels, biliary structures).  
- Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume or ratio.  
- Status of any pre‑operative systemic chemotherapy (has it been given, and response).  
- Assessment of hepatic parenchymal quality (steatosis, fibrosis) that could affect FLR tolerance.

A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).

• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance (Minagawa et al.)

B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)

D. Results of liver specific imaging (MRI/CT) to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.
E. Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered – impacts the timing and total duration of peri operative treatment. 
F. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

- Post‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX) should be administered as adjuvant treatment, given the KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective).  
- Schedule regular surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 2 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential clinical information is lacking for a reliable recommendation; the primary tumor and liver metastasis are both clearly resectable based on the data provided.

Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate short‑course radiotherapy for the upper rectal tumor (5 Gy × 5 days).  
- After a 1–2 week interval, proceed with total mesorectal excision (TME).  
- Plan a synchronous liver resection (segment III wedge or segmentectomy) at the time of TME, provided operative time and patient condition are acceptable; alternatively, schedule a staged liver resection 4–6 weeks after TME if intra‑operative logistics or patient factors favor separation.  
- Incorporate peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX) either before the combined operation (as neoadjuvant) or after (adjuvant), to address micrometastatic disease; consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type, if high‑risk features are present.  
- Continue postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging per standard colorectal liver metastasis follow‑up protocols.  

Step 2 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative liver function (bilirubin, albumin, INR, indocyanine‑green clearance) and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Comprehensive cardiopulmonary fitness assessment (ejection fraction, pulmonary function tests) to confirm tolerance of combined abdominal surgery.  
- Detailed mesorectal fascia status on MRI (distance to circumferential resection margin) to confirm feasibility of sphincter‑preserving TME.  
- Full staging CT of chest and abdomen to exclude additional extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (e.g., cardiovascular, pulmonary) influencing surgical risk.

Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 3 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX; add bevacizumab given KRAS mutation and BRAF wild‑type).  
- Perform baseline restaging after chemotherapy with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI and repeat CEA measurement to assess tumor response and exclude new extra‑hepatic disease.  
- If imaging confirms that all three liver lesions remain resectable and no new metastases appear, proceed to simultaneous resection of the transverse colon primary (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy) and liver metastases (anatomical segmentectomy of IV, V and VI or non‑anatomical wedge resections ensuring a future liver remnant ≥ 30 % in this 72‑year‑old).  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months systemic therapy, adjusting regimen based on pathological response and tolerability.  

Step 2 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Detailed staging of the primary tumor (T‑stage, N‑stage, presence of mesocolic fascia involvement).  
- Quantitative liver volumetry to confirm adequate future liver remnant.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assessment for steatosis or fibrosis.  
- Confirmation that there are no occult extra‑hepatic metastases (e.g., lung, peritoneum) on full staging work‑up.

Step 1 – Oncological strategy  
- Confirm complete staging: contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease; obtain liver volumetry to verify that the future liver remnant (FLR) will be ≥30 % (≥40 % if pre‑operative chemotherapy is given).  
- Because the three metastases are ≤3 cm, located in segments IV, V and VI with only partial contact to the right portal branch and no vascular invasion, a minor hepatectomy (segment IVb wedge + non‑anatomic resections of segments V and VI) can achieve R0 resection while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments.  
- Offer peri‑operative systemic therapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 cycles before surgery (“neoadjuvant” or “peri‑operative” chemotherapy). KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents; bevacizumab is appropriate. This short course provides a “proof of time” to assess tumor biology and may improve disease‑free survival.  
- Re‑stage after chemotherapy (CT/MRI). If disease remains resectable and no new lesions appear, proceed to a simultaneous resection of the transverse colon primary (right hemicolectomy) and the liver metastases in the same operative session, provided the patient’s operative risk is acceptable.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of a 6‑month total course) should be given, tailored to tolerance, to address micrometastatic disease.  
- Follow‑up: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of the liver and chest every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 2 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The hepatic disease meets technical criteria (ability to obtain R0 margins, preservation of ≥2 contiguous segments, adequate FLR) and there is no documented extra‑hepatic spread. Therefore surgery can be performed immediately, although a short course of neoadjuvant chemotherapy is recommended for biological selection.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Performance status / ECOG or ASA classification.  
- Detailed comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary, renal, hepatic function).  
- Precise FLR calculation (volumetric data).  
- Full thoracic staging (CT or PET‑CT) to rule out lung metastases.  
- Baseline laboratory values (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) to assess liver synthetic reserve.  
- Details of the primary tumour depth (T stage) and nodal status (N stage).  
- Patient’s preference regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.

- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to be considered based on pathological response and final staging.

Step 2 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: resection is feasible but requires (a) confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease on chest imaging and (b) definitive FLR volume assessment to ensure safe hepatic resection. Until these prerequisites are fulfilled, surgery cannot be scheduled upfront.

- Detailed arterial and portal venous anatomy of the liver lesions (extent of portal branch contact, arterial supply).  
- Quantitative FLR ratio or volumetric analysis.  
- Results of thoracic imaging (chest CT) for pulmonary metastases.  
- Presence or absence of bone or brain metastases (imaging not reported).  
- Information on any systemic therapy already administered.  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and baseline liver function.

According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered resectable.

A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Patient’s general condition and comorbidities influencing tolerance of combined surgery.
F. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 – Oncological strategy  
- Confirm baseline staging: complete blood count, liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, and cardiopulmonary assessment (e.g., VO2 max or CPET) to ensure fitness for major surgery.  
- Initiate peri‑operative systemic therapy because the disease is technically resectable but biologically aggressive (CEA 200 ng/mL). Preferred regimen: 3 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS‑wild‑type left‑sided primary.  
- Restaging contrast‑enhanced CT (or MRI) after chemotherapy to verify that all liver lesions remain resectable and that no new extra‑hepatic disease has appeared.  
- If restaging confirms resectability, proceed to simultaneous resection of the sigmoid primary (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy) and liver metastases using a parenchymal‑sparing approach (multiple wedge resections/segmentectomies of segments II, III, V, VIII) aiming to preserve ≥30 % future liver remnant.  
- Complete the planned systemic therapy to a total of 6 months (adjuvant phase) after surgery, adjusting based on postoperative pathology and tolerance.  

Step 2 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  

Step 3 – Missing data  
No critical data are lacking for a provisional recommendation; however, the following information should be confirmed before definitive surgical planning:  
- Quantitative liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and calculation of future liver remnant volume.  
- Patient’s performance status and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Detailed relationship of each metastasis to major hepatic vessels (to ensure safe margin‑negative resection).

Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated disease and the need for micrometastatic control.  
- Administer 2–3 months (≈ 8 cycles) of chemotherapy, then repeat high‑resolution liver MRI and CT of chest/abdomen to assess radiologic response and confirm that the two hepatic lesions remain resectable.  
- If imaging shows stable or responding disease and adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver), proceed to surgical resection.  
- Surgical plan: simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) and parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (segment II and segment IVa wedge/segmentectomy) preserving the middle hepatic vein.  
- If intra‑operative assessment suggests excessive operative stress (e.g., poor performance status, extensive adhesions) or if postoperative recovery after the colon resection is expected to be prolonged, convert to a staged approach: (1) right hemicolectomy, recover 4–6 weeks, (2) repeat chemotherapy if needed, then (3) liver resection.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy, with consideration of adding a targeted agent (bevacizumab) if not given pre‑operatively.

Step 2 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – resection requires completion of neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (and confirmation of adequate FLR) before definitive surgery.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelets) and indocyanine‑green clearance if available.  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant (CT‑based or MRI‑based).  
- Detailed chest imaging to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Exact number and location of regional lymph nodes involved (extent of N2 disease).  
- Comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, cardiovascular disease) that may influence operative risk.

- Immediate neurological priority: evaluate the cerebellar lesion for surgical resection or stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) plus corticosteroids; choose the modality based on size, symptomatic status, and accessibility.

   • Second, proceed to hepatic resection (anatomical or non‑anatomical) aiming for R0 margins; consider portal vein embolization beforehand if FLR is marginal.  
- Continue postoperative systemic therapy (maintenance or further conversion regimen) and consider adjuvant radiotherapy to the cerebellar bed if indicated.  

Step 2 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: current liver disease is multiple and bilobar, requiring downsizing chemotherapy and confirmation of adequate future liver remnant; definitive resection also depends on successful control of the cerebellar metastasis.

- Size, exact location, and symptomatology of the cerebellar metastasis; feasibility of surgical resection versus SRS.

Step 1 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) given the high tumor burden (four liver lesions + pelvic peritoneal implants) and wild‑type BRAF.

   • Simultaneous or staged colorectal primary resection (depending on symptoms or obstruction).  
   • Anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing liver resection aiming for ≥ 30 % future liver remnant (or ≥ 40 % if underlying liver disease).  
   • Cytoreductive surgery (CRS) of pelvic peritoneal implants with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) if complete cytoreduction (CC‑0/1) appears feasible.  
- If response is insufficient or disease remains extensive, continue systemic therapy and consider palliative options (targeted agents, clinical trial, best supportive care).  

Step 2 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – resection is contingent on (a) demonstrable tumor response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and (b) definitive imaging data (liver lesion distribution, FLR calculation, PCI) that confirm the possibility of achieving R0 liver resection and complete peritoneal cytoreduction.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Exact size, segmental location and vascular proximity of each liver metastasis.  
- Planned future liver remnant volume or liver function assessment (ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh).  
- Detailed peritoneal disease burden (PCI score, exact sites of implants).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver function.  
- KRAS/NRAS mutational status (relevant for anti‑EGFR therapy).  
- Symptoms or obstruction related to the rectosigmoid primary (necessitating urgent resection).  
These data are essential to confirm whether an R0 liver resection and complete CRS‑HIPEC are technically feasible.
